title: Vector triple product and cross-product equations
terms: vector triple product; BAC-CAB identity; cross-product equation.

exposition.text:
The vector triple product identity is a × (b × c) = b(a · c) − c(a · b). It shows explicitly that
cross products are not associative and reduces nested cross products to dot products and scalar
multiplication. The related expression (a × b) × c = b(a · c) − a(b · c) has a different arrangement.
To solve a × v = b with a ̸= 0, a necessary condition is a · b = 0. When this holds, all solutions
2
are v = −(a × b)/∥a∥ + ta. The free component parallel to a is invisible to crossing with a. If
one also requires v ⊥ a, the solution is unique.

x(x · a) = a, so ∥x∥ = 1. Consequently ∥b∥ = ∥a × x∥ = ∥a∥. Conversely, if the lengths

agree, x = (b × a)/∥a∥ is perpendicular to a, has norm one, and satisfies both equations by
the triple-product identity.

question.text:
Unit vectors a, b satisfy a · b = 1/2. What is a × (b × a)?
1 1 1 1
(A) a − b (B) b − a (C) a − b (D) a + b (E) (a + b)
2 2 2 2

solution.text: Apply the triple-product identity with c = a: a × (b × a) = b(a · a) − a(a · b) = b − a/2.

question.text:
If (a × b) · c = 3, what is (a × b) × (a × c)?
(A) 3a (B) −3a (C) 3b (D) 3c (E) 0

solution.text:
Apply BAC-CAB with first vector a × b, second vector a, and third vector c. The result is
a[(a × b) · c] − c[(a × b) · a] = 3a. The zero second scalar follows from perpendicularity. This
connects vector and scalar triple products without coordinates.
